articles.title: NASA’s Roman space telescope heads to deep space after surviving budget cuts
articles.summary:

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope survived two White House attempts to cancel it and is now on its way to a […]
The post NASA’s Roman space telescope heads to deep space after surviving budget cuts first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

A space telescope with 100 times the sky coverage of Hubble lifted off from Florida this past Sunday. Astronomers have been waiting nearly a decade for this.

The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope survived two White House attempts to cancel it and is now on its way to a stable orbit roughly one million miles from Earth, the same region where the James Webb Space Telescope operates. The price tag was $4.3 billion. The camera is 300 megapixels. The mission is to answer questions about the universe that current telescopes can’t get to.

What Roman can do that Hubble and Webb cannot

Roman isn’t a replacement for Hubble or Webb; rather, it works alongside them at a scale neither was designed for.

Its camera matches Hubble’s sharpness and resolution but covers a field of view at least 100 times larger. Each image captures a patch of sky roughly one and a half times wider than a full moon looks from Earth. Less zoom lens, more wide-angle survey camera. That scale matters: it can cover in a single pass what would take Hubble years to piece together from separate observations.

Roman also carries a coronagraph, an instrument that blocks the glare of nearby stars so scientists can photograph the planets orbiting them more clearly. NASA expects it to photograph “giant worlds that are older, colder, and in closer orbits” than the ones direct imaging has mostly caught so far.

A layered system with Hubble and Webb

The three telescopes work in layers. Roman sweeps wide, picking out targets across billions of galaxies. Hubble follows up with infrared, visible, and ultraviolet light for a fuller picture. Webb goes deepest, with its larger mirror and superior resolution.

Roman can also observe the surrounding areas when Hubble or Webb are zoomed in on something, adding context to what the others see. They each do what the others can’t.

All of Roman’s imagery will be released to the public as it comes in. NASA expects that to start in early 2027, after months of calibration in its final orbit.

The question the mission was built to answer

The universe is not just expanding; its rate of expansion is way faster than it should be. Scientists noticed this at the end of the last century and have never fully explained it. Roman was built to gather the data to try.

“It’s like if you were to throw a ball in the air, and instead of the ball coming back down, it just keeps shooting away,” said Julie McEnery, the telescope’s senior project scientist. “There’s something really fundamental that we don’t understand about the nature of our universe itself, and Roman is purpose-built to address and provide the data that we need to address these questions.”

Dark matter, dark energy, black holes, planetary formation, galaxies by the billions; the initial mission runs five years and could extend to ten.

A close call for American science

This launch almost didn’t happen. A 2025 White House proposal called for what analysts described as “extinction level cuts” to NASA’s science budget, with the Roman mission among the targets. Congress rejected the plan and restored the agency’s 2026 funding to $24.4 billion.

The current administration is now pushing a 23 percent reduction in NASA’s overall 2027 budget, to $18.8 billion, along with a 46 percent cut to science programs. The Planetary Society says that would terminate more than 50 missions.

For now, Roman is in space. Named for Nancy Grace Roman, NASA’s first chief of astronomy, who died in 2018, the telescope spent nearly a decade in development before final approval and construction began in 2020. McEnery spoke at the post-launch press conference: “It feels like I’m on the edge of a precipice, and we’re just about to set a foot off into the unknown.”

Sunday’s launch was also the last flight of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket. The company is retiring it to concentrate on Starship.

articles.personality_title: NASA’s Roman Space Telescope launched to explore universe’s biggest mysteries
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA has developed a new space telescope named after Nancy Grace Roman, its first chief of astronomy. This telescope is designed to study the universe in ways that previous telescopes like Hubble and Webb cannot. It took nearly ten years to build and faced serious budget threats before finally being launched.

**What happened** – On Sunday, the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope was launched from Florida. It is now heading to a stable orbit about one million miles from Earth, near where the James Webb Space Telescope operates. The launch used SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy rocket, which will be retired after this mission. The telescope has a 300-megapixel camera and special instruments to study distant galaxies and planets.

**Impact** – Roman can take pictures of the sky that cover 100 times more area than Hubble’s camera. This wide view will help scientists study the universe’s expansion, which is happening faster than expected, a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades. Roman will also help find and photograph planets around other stars using a tool that blocks star glare. Its work will complement Hubble and Webb by covering large areas while the others focus on smaller, detailed views.

**What's next step** – After reaching its orbit, Roman will spend several months calibrating its instruments. NASA plans to start releasing the telescope’s images to the public by early 2027. The mission is set to last at least five years, with the possibility of extending to ten, during which it will collect data to help explain dark energy, dark matter, black holes, and galaxy formation.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope’s launch marks a major step forward in exploring cosmic mysteries by combining wide sky coverage with powerful new technology, promising fresh insights into how the universe works.

articles.title: ‘Not-quite primordial’ black holes may explain baffling JWST discovery
articles.summary: The James Webb Space Telescope seems to have discovered more ancient black holes than theory had predicted, and now we have a new way to explain why
articles.content:
The James Webb Space Telescope seems to have discovered more ancient black holes than theory had predicted, and now we have a new way to explain why

The James Webb Space Telescope has discovered plenty of little red dot galaxies NASA, ESA, CSA, STScI, and D. Kocevski (Colby U.)/Space Telescope Science Institute Office of Public Outreach

There may have been black holes in the early universe before the first stars, and a group of theoretical physicists has proposed a new way to explain how they could have formed using the heat of the cosmic microwave background. The idea may be a better explanation for the “little red dots” identified by the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) – distant galaxies that seem to host surprisingly large numbers of astonishingly ancient black holes.

“James Webb is discovering many more black holes than most of us theorists predicted in our most optimistic models,” says Priyamvada Natarajan at Yale University. “The universe is just littered with black holes.”

An existing idea is that primordial black holes formed in violent space-time spasms in the early universe before any stars appeared. But these violent spasms are hard to reconcile with the milder ripples that astronomers see in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), faint light left over from the primordial universe. Theorists have had to propose complicated new physical laws to make the explanation fit.

Advertisement

Wenzer Qin and Neal Weiner at New York University and Soubhik Kumar at Tufts University in Massachusetts realised there was another option. They began by assuming milder ripples of dark matter moved through the early universe, and argued that large black holes would be able to form inside clumps of this dark matter, with the hot CMB keeping gas and dust from collapsing into smaller ones instead.

They call these black holes “not-quite-primordial” and argue they provide an explanation for the black holes spotted via the JWST that doesn’t require drastic changes to cosmologists’ picture of the early universe.

The researchers reached out to Natarajan, a theoretical astrophysicist, to help confirm their logic.

“This is a case where you could actually have a black hole forming before the stars. And that I found really exciting,” says Natarajan.

Subscriber-only newsletter Sign up to Lost in Space-Time Sign up to newsletter

“What’s nice about the model is that it invokes less speculative physics than traditional primordial black hole physics,” says John Regan at Maynooth University, Ireland, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Having says that, what we need ultimately will be concrete observations. We’ll need to see some ultra-early-Universe signatures of black holes, be that from gravitational waves or from some future CMB observations, to see if black holes truly existed at the very earliest times.”

Qin and collaborators are getting ready for those observations. Their next step will be to simulate the new process and see what it implies about the spectrum of light that should be emitted from around a not-quite-primordial black hole. They can then compare these predictions more closely to data from JWST.

They are also looking forward to future satellite telescopes like the proposed Primordial Inflation Explorer (PIXIE), which should be able to measure the CMB spectrum well enough to find evidence for their proposal.

articles.personality_title: New theory explains unexpected ancient black holes found by James Webb Telescope
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) has found more ancient black holes in distant galaxies than scientists expected. These black holes appear in the early universe, even before the first stars formed, which challenges existing ideas about how black holes came to be.

**What happened** – A team of physicists from New York University and Tufts University proposed a new explanation. They suggest that “not-quite-primordial” black holes formed inside clumps of dark matter, helped by the heat of leftover light from the Big Bang called the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This idea avoids using complicated new physics and fits better with what astronomers see.

**Impact** – This new model helps explain the surprising number of black holes the JWST found without needing to change our understanding of the early universe too much. It offers a simpler way to understand how big black holes could form before stars existed, filling a gap in our knowledge about the universe’s first moments.

**What’s next step** – The researchers will run simulations to predict the light patterns that these black holes might create. They will compare these predictions with JWST data to test their idea. They also look forward to future space missions like the Primordial Inflation Explorer (PIXIE) that could provide more evidence by measuring the cosmic microwave background in detail.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists have proposed a new way that ancient black holes could have formed early in the universe, helping explain surprising discoveries made by the James Webb Space Telescope.
articles.personality_title_fr: Une nouvelle théorie explique les anciens trous noirs inattendus découverts par le télescope James Webb
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le télescope spatial James Webb (JWST) a découvert plus de trous noirs anciens dans des galaxies lointaines que ce que les scientifiques avaient prévu. Ces trous noirs semblent exister dans l’univers très tôt, avant même la formation des premières étoiles, ce qui remet en question les idées actuelles sur leur origine.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une équipe de physiciens de l’Université de New York et de l’Université Tufts a proposé une nouvelle explication. Ils suggèrent que des trous noirs « presque primordiaux » se sont formés à l’intérieur de regroupements de matière noire, aidés par la chaleur de la lumière résiduelle du Big Bang appelée fond diffus cosmologique (CMB). Cette idée évite de recourir à une physique trop compliquée et correspond mieux aux observations.

**Impact** – Ce nouveau modèle permet d’expliquer le nombre surprenant de trous noirs découverts par le JWST sans modifier trop notre compréhension de l’univers primordial. Il offre une manière plus simple de comprendre comment de gros trous noirs ont pu apparaître avant les étoiles, comblant ainsi une lacune dans nos connaissances sur les premiers instants de l’univers.

**Prochaine étape** – Les chercheurs vont réaliser des simulations pour prédire les types de lumière émis par ces trous noirs. Ils compareront ensuite ces prédictions aux données du JWST pour vérifier leur théorie. Ils attendent aussi avec impatience des missions spatiales futures comme le Primordial Inflation Explorer (PIXIE) qui pourraient fournir plus de preuves en mesurant précisément le fond diffus cosmologique.

**Phrase clé** – Des scientifiques ont proposé une nouvelle façon dont les anciens trous noirs ont pu se former tôt dans l’univers, ce qui aide à expliquer les découvertes surprenantes du télescope James Webb.
articles.personality_title_es: Nueva teoría explica antiguos agujeros negros inesperados descubiertos por el telescopio James Webb
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El telescopio espacial James Webb (JWST) ha encontrado más agujeros negros antiguos en galaxias lejanas de lo que los científicos esperaban. Estos agujeros negros parecen existir en el universo temprano, incluso antes de que se formaran las primeras estrellas, lo que desafía las ideas actuales sobre cómo se formaron.

**Qué pasó** – Un equipo de físicos de la Universidad de Nueva York y la Universidad Tufts propuso una nueva explicación. Sugieren que los agujeros negros “casi primordiales” se formaron dentro de grupos de materia oscura, ayudados por el calor de la luz sobrante del Big Bang llamada fondo cósmico de microondas (CMB). Esta idea evita usar física complicada y encaja mejor con lo que los astrónomos observan.

**Impacto** – Este nuevo modelo ayuda a explicar el sorprendente número de agujeros negros que encontró el JWST sin necesitar cambiar demasiado nuestra comprensión del universo temprano. Ofrece una forma más sencilla de entender cómo grandes agujeros negros pudieron formarse antes que las estrellas, llenando un vacío en nuestro conocimiento sobre los primeros momentos del universo.

**Próximo paso** – Los investigadores harán simulaciones para predecir los patrones de luz que estos agujeros negros podrían crear. Compararán estas predicciones con los datos del JWST para probar su idea. También esperan futuras misiones espaciales como el Explorador de la Inflación Primordial (PIXIE), que podrían proporcionar más evidencia al medir el fondo cósmico de microondas en detalle.

**Frase clave** – Científicos han propuesto una nueva forma en que los antiguos agujeros negros podrían haberse formado temprano en el universo, ayudando a explicar los sorprendentes descubrimientos del telescopio James Webb.
